title: The Leeward Passage
premise: Rosalind Villalobos, a riverboat captain hiding under a borrowed name, is hired to resupply an expedition that has gone silent deep upriver. She finds the survivors guarding a discovery the government will drown in paperwork and blood: proof that the drowned town of her childhood — the one that took her family — was destroyed deliberately, not by flood. To bring the expedition home, Rosalind must run the river past the very officials who erased her past, choosing between the justice of exposure and the safety of everyone aboard. She delivers the truth to a journalist in the delta, surrendering her anonymity at last, and the river that made her invisible finally carries her name downstream.
about_author: Edmund Dunmore is the pen name of a former merchant-marine officer who spent a decade piloting shallow-draft vessels on remote inland waterways before turning to fiction. He writes adventure novels about people whose livelihoods depend on reading water, weather, and other people's silences.

chapters.title: Dead Water at Dawn
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. A routine fuel run downriver establishes her world: the boat, the debt, the compass her father left, and the careful invisibility of a woman living under another name. A government man named Corrigan hires her at triple rate to check on a silent expedition. Beat: unease beneath routine — she knows rivers punish curiosity.

chapters.title: The Hush Above the Bend
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. She ascends the narrowing river, reading sandbars and abandoned camps, finding the expedition's supply cache looted and their radio mast snapped, not fallen. Flashbacks surface: the flood that drowned San Esteban and her family when she was twelve. Beat: dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: What the Surveyors Kept
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, with a letter from expedition leader Dr. Amara Osei. She finds three survivors — Osei, a wounded surveyor, and a terrified junior — holed up in a mission ruin. Osei shows her sonar maps: the old dam upstream was dynamited in '61, the flood engineered to bury a land scandal. Beat: the past becomes evidence.

chapters.title: Corrigan's Ledger
chapters.summary: Osei's POV. Flashback chapters from the expedition reveal how Corrigan's agency funded their survey, then tried to confiscate the maps; the fourth team member died refusing to hand them over. The survivors trust Rosalind with the truth — and the plates. Beat: complicity and grief; the weight of knowing.

chapters.title: Running the Narrows
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The descent begins with a patrol boat behind them and the season's first storm ahead. Rosalind threads an uncharted channel she alone remembers, buying a night's lead. The wounded surveyor worsens. Beat: competence as survival; the river as ally.

chapters.title: The Man Who Drowned a Town
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Corrigan corners them at a fuel depot, offering amnesty for the maps — and revealing he knows her real name, that her father was the engineer who refused to open the dam gates. Rosalind stalls, lies, and signs nothing. Beat: fury and recognition; her invisibility was engineered too.

chapters.title: High Water
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The storm hits at the worst reach of the river. Corrigan's launch pursues them into floodwater; a collision cripples his boat, and Rosalind, against every instinct, turns back to pull him from the water. Beat: the moral center of the book — justice is not drowning your enemy.

chapters.title: The Compass Points Home
chapters.summary: Osei's POV. Adrift and hunted, the survivors argue: sell the story, bury it, or burn it. Rosalind finally tells them who she is — the girl from San Esteban. Osei realizes the maps are not just evidence but testimony, and testimony needs a living witness. Beat: identity claimed, not confessed.

chapters.title: The Leeward Passage
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The climax: a night run through the delta's leeward channels as Corrigan's remaining men and the agency close in. She splits the group, uses her boat as a decoy, nearly loses it — and nearly herself — in the marsh. The plates reach a delta journalist at dawn. Beat: sacrifice, terror, triumph.

chapters.title: Names on the Water
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, months later. The story breaks; hearings begin; Corrigan, spared by her own hand, testifies to save himself. Rosalind signs her true name to the witness ledger and renames her boat San Esteban. The river carries her past the drowned town one last time. Beat: quiet resolution — memory surfaced, justice begun, self reclaimed.
